children: By Staff Writer

UAE state-owned utility Etihad Water and Electricity (EtihadWE) is planning to interconnect water transmission networks across the eastern and western Northern Emirates to strengthen supply security and improve resilience against potential disruptions in the Gulf.

Chief Operating Officer Abdulla Al-Khemeiri told Zawya Projects that the utility is considering network expansions and additional pumping infrastructure to enable water transfers between the two regions.
"Resilience of the system is now our priority, so we are going to integrate the east and west coasts. That gives more resilience and flexibility in case of issues in the Gulf," he said.
The eastern region is currently supplied entirely by EtihadWE, while the western region also receives support from Abu Dhabi's TAQA.
However, the mountainous terrain separating the two regions presents significant engineering challenges, requiring higher pumping pressure to transfer water across the network.
The proposed expansions would strengthen transmission capacity and enable water transfers from multiple locations, he said.
The utility was also considering further investments in Fujairah, where it sees opportunities for future expansion, he added.

In May 2026, the development and investment arm of EtihadWE had signed an Engineering, Procurement and Construction (EPC) agreement with NMDC Infra and Lantania Aguas for the 60MIGD Fujairah I Independent Water Producer (IWP) project. The 60 million imperial gallons per day (MIGD) seawater reverse osmosis (SWRO) desalination plant is being developed with a total investment value of 1.046 billion UAE dirhams ($285 million).
Water storage
While geo-political disruptions have not significantly affected EtihadWE's operations, the utility is strengthening contingency measures to address potential future risks.
The utility has developed water storage capacity equivalent to approximately three days of current consumption, exceeding the minimum one-day storage requirement.
"We now consume around 200 million imperial gallons per day (MIGD) and have storage of around 600 million imperial gallons, so three times. That covers at least three days," Al-Khemeiri said.
The additional storage provides a buffer against potential interruptions to water production or transmission.
“When we built the storage, we changed the strategy to build more capacity than required,” he explained. “This gives more resilience to the network.”
The utility had also implemented underground water storage based on groundwater wells/aquifers to provide alternative sources of supply during emergencies.
“The water is drinkable, with TDS within the limit. So we leverage these underground reservoirs for resilience too,” he said.
Desalination efficiency and supply chain localisation

EtihadWE is an equity holder and offtaker for the AED 2.5 billion ($681 million) NAQA'A reverse osmosis desalination plant, which has a production capacity of 681,900 m3/day and can meet the water needs of more than two million people.

Al-Khemeiri said the plant, located in the emirate of Umm Al Quwain, operates at an energy consumption level of 2.98 kilowatt-hours per cubic metre (kWh/m³), supported by pressure exchangers that recover energy from the desalination process and variable frequency drives that regulate motor and pump speeds.

The utility is also examining opportunities to localise the supply and production of water treatment chemicals, a major operational cost, to reduce dependence on imported materials and strengthen supply chain resilience.
"If we can source them within the UAE, or establish production here, that would take a lot of pressure off, minimise risk and maximise benefit," he said.
EtihadWE has also signed memoranda of understanding with Khalifa University and other institutions to study potential uses for desalination brine.
Smart metering and water loss reduction
Al-Khemeiri said EtihadWE had completed the installation of smart electricity and water meters across its customer base, with approximately 70 percent integrated into its back-office systems.
The utility is also deploying district metered areas (DMAs) to monitor water flows and identify distribution losses.
"We are installing DMAs in different zones and areas to monitor what is coming in and what is going to the customers," he said.
EtihadWE has reduced water losses by around 10 percent over the past three years and is targeting a non-revenue water level below 15 percent by 2030, he added.
(Reporting by Anoop Menon; Editing by SA Kader)
